Start with your own environment

What do you need to know about your stack?

The deployment passed, but the app still fails. The hosting domain changed, but the login callback didn’t. Finding the cause means checking more than one service. You can also check those settings before a change.

01

What does this service connect to?

Ask your agent to compare configuration across services. Have it show the settings behind its answer, identify the environment, and say what it couldn’t check.

02

What changed around this failure?

Compare deployment records, audit events, or saved snapshots. Today’s settings alone don’t show what changed.

03

What should I check before changing this?

Before changing a domain, compare hosting settings, DNS records, and login callbacks. Ask which services were checked and what still needs checking. Then verify the result after the change.

Connect your agent and try a question →

One catalog, two ways to work

Check that the change worked.

Read back the configuration after a change. Ask your agent to show the values behind its conclusion and say what it couldn’t check. You can inspect and repeat those commands in the terminal. A successful API response doesn’t prove the integration works.

01 / Add

Add the API you need.

Have an internal deployment API with docs but no schema? Ask your agent to write a supported OpenAPI document, validate and import it, and test a generated command. Keep it alongside your vendor commands.

When there is no published schema →
02 / Run

Use the same commands as your agent.

Find a command, fill in its inputs, and run it in the TUI. Inspect the response and execution logs as you work.

Explore the TUI →
03 / Correct

Fix a command that fails.

Your agent can update a generated command or its connection settings through MCP. Inspect the change and retry. The agent supplies the diagnosis and correction.

See catalog repair →
04 / Repeat

Keep a task you will use again.

Save tested HTTP commands as a reusable workflow. You and your agent can also use what you learn to write clients, tests, and infrastructure in your development tools.

Practical questions

What you need to get started.

The API access guide covers installation, MCP connection, importing a schema, and making a first call.

Does the API need to publish an OpenAPI document?

No. Your agent can write a supported document from API docs or request examples. Validate it and test the generated commands before relying on them.

Can I use Oatty without an agent?

Yes. Search the catalog, use autocomplete, execute commands, and inspect results in the TUI.

Does Oatty include its own language model?

No. You connect your own agent. Oatty provides the catalog, command execution, results, and workflows.

What changes when a command is repaired?

Oatty changes the generated command definition. It doesn’t rewrite the API provider’s OpenAPI document.

How do I configure authentication?

The current source supports catalog request headers with raw, environment, file, or secret-backed values. Check your installed release and the API’s requirements. Native OAuth token refresh has not been established.

The next task

Keep the commands you’ll need again.

Your catalog stays available as you add services and take on new tasks. Reuse the commands that worked, check the current configuration, and save useful HTTP sequences as workflows.
